method: Our professor provided feedback on our Access Riders. This allowed me to better understand their applications and practical methods, how to compose an Access Rider, and how to consider the core questions behind it. We also examined an academic paper closely in class. From this paper, I came to realise that accessibility is not merely a piece of technology for solving practical problems. On the contrary, it is an aesthetic form in its own right that expands the boundaries of human sensory experience and artistic perception. Contemporary disabled artists are challenging traditional assumptions around accessibility. They produce nuanced artistic creations and re‑frame accessibility as a highly creative artistic medium
related_work:
1.Alt-Text as Poetry（Finnegan Shannon and Bojana Cokylat）
In this project, writing alt-text is no longer seen as boring coding, but as writing poetry. For the same photo, instead of the dry description "a photo of a sunset", people are encouraged to capture its light, mood and texture — like "pink and purple sunset hues spread across the sky like a watercolor painting".
This has completely changed my view on accessible design. It should never be just an afterthought patch, nor a cold line of code rule. Designers ought to turn plain details into something that carries feeling.
2. Audimance（Kinetic Light）
Usually, the spoken descriptions for blind or low-vision theatre audiences are plain and flat — just simple reports like: “The dancer raises their right hand,” “The wheelchair moves forward.”
But disabled dance company Kinetic Light created an app called Audimance that changes everything. It turns dry descriptions into a rich, multi-layered soundscape.
With this app, you don’t just hear plain facts. You hear wheels brushing the floor, dancers’ steady breaths, the beat of the music, and poetic words woven together. You can explore different sound layers on your own — turning a dance you used to only “see” into something you feel all around you.
This showed me clearly: accessibility itself can be beautiful, vivid art.（ Kinetic Light, "Imagining the Future of Audio Description": kineticlight.org/audimance (accessed 1 August 2023).）
references:
Kinetic Light, "Imagining the Future of Audio Description": kineticlight.org/audimance (accessed 1 August 2023)
Tobin Siebers, "Disability Aesthetics," PMLA 120, No. 2 (2005) p. 543
Finnegan Shannon and Bojana Coklyat, "Alt Text as Poetry": alt-text-as-poetry.net/ (accessed 3 September 2023).
conclusion_future_work:
Through this class, I realise that when we create art and design work, we usually think first about the experience and needs of most people. But this will leave some people’s feelings out without us noticing.
As designers and artists, we should not look at works from only one point of view. We need to think in many different ways. We need to care about the feelings of most people, and also see the needs of minority groups. When I create works in the future, I should think about the experience of different people from the very beginning.
title: Explanation of Terms
introduction:
1. Participatory Audio Description
Standard audio description is usually factual, one-way spoken narration made for blind and low vision audiences. Participatory audio description reworks this tool into a shared and creative project. It invites users, artists, and disabled people to take an active part in writing the descriptions—turning a tool that is normally meant to be neutral and clear into a medium for personal, poetic artistic expression.
2.Access Aesthetics
Traditional accessibility facilities—such as rigid translations or descriptions for the blind or deaf—are often seen as “add-ons” separate from artworks. “Accessible Aesthetics,”  holds that these can be expressive, interpretive, and even transformative creations. It challenges conventional ableist beauty standards, arguing that the lived experiences of disabled people, their assistive tools, and how they engage with the world hold unique beauty and creativity in themselves.
Tobin Siebers, "Disability Aesthetics," PMLA 120, No. 2 (2005) p. 543
